reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Digestive System Tumours
clinicalPearls: A spectrum of mucin-producing appendiceal epithelial tumours ranging from low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm (LAMN) through high-grade (HAMN) to invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma.
Often discovered incidentally on imaging as a distended, mucin-filled appendix (mucocele) or at appendicectomy for presumed appendicitis.
The defining hazard is peritoneal dissemination producing pseudomyxoma peritonei, a slowly progressive accumulation of gelatinous mucin with epithelial cells throughout the peritoneal cavity.
LAMN is characterised by pushing, expansile growth with loss of the muscularis mucosae and absence of infiltrative invasion, distinguishing it from frank adenocarcinoma.
CT typically shows a cystic tubular appendiceal mass, sometimes with mural calcification; rupture or extra-appendiceal mucin greatly raises the risk of peritoneal spread.
Because puncture or piecemeal removal can seed the peritoneum, an intact en bloc appendicectomy without rupture is essential, and biopsy of a suspected mucocele is avoided.
Pathological reporting must document tumour grade, margin status, presence of acellular versus cellular mucin beyond the appendix, and any perforation, as these drive prognosis and follow-up.
Established peritoneal disease is managed in specialist centres with cytoreductive surgery combined with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy where appropriate.
reference.pathophysiology: Appendiceal mucinous neoplasms arise from the appendiceal epithelium, which undergoes mucinous transformation, frequently driven by mutations in KRAS and GNAS that stimulate abundant mucin production. Progressive intraluminal mucin accumulation dilates the appendix to form a mucocele and raises intraluminal pressure, which may cause the wall to thin, ulcerate and eventually rupture. When neoplastic mucin-producing epithelial cells escape into the peritoneal cavity, they redistribute along the flow of peritoneal fluid and implant preferentially at sites of fluid resorption, secreting copious mucin to produce pseudomyxoma peritonei. Even low-grade lesions, despite bland cytology and lack of true stromal invasion, can be lethal through this relentless peritoneal mucinous accumulation causing progressive abdominal distension, adhesions and bowel compromise.
additionalDifferentials: ovarian mucinous neoplasm with peritoneal spread
additionalInvestigations: contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis
MRI to map peritoneal and mucinous disease burden
colonoscopy to exclude a synchronous colorectal primary
tumour markers including CEA, CA19-9 and CA125 for baseline and monitoring
histopathological grading with mucin cellularity assessment
molecular testing for KRAS and GNAS where diagnosis is uncertain
diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal assessment in selected cases
redFlags: appendiceal rupture or free intraperitoneal mucin on imaging
new or progressive abdominal distension suggesting pseudomyxoma peritonei
cellular mucin beyond the appendiceal wall on histology
bowel obstruction from peritoneal mucinous disease
reference.prognosis: Localised, intact low-grade lesions confined to the appendix and completely excised have an excellent outlook, whereas peritoneal dissemination markedly worsens prognosis, with survival strongly dependent on tumour grade and completeness of cytoreduction. High-grade and invasive tumours carry a considerably poorer outcome.
pitfalls: Rupturing or aspirating a suspected mucocele, seeding the peritoneum with mucin-producing cells.
Dismissing acellular peritoneal mucin as harmless without thorough sampling for epithelial cells.
Treating pseudomyxoma peritonei as ovarian in origin when the appendix is the true primary.
Under-reporting margin, perforation and mucin cellularity, which are essential for risk stratification.
Delaying referral to a specialist peritoneal malignancy centre once dissemination is suspected.
